content: 1. Pyrazinamide (Z) is dosed at 35–40 mg/kg, while Ethambutol (E) is dosed at 20 mg/kg, with a range of 15–25 mg/kg. For isoniazid, the higher end of the dosing range is more appropriate for younger children, whereas older children should receive doses at the lower end of the range. 2. The recommended dosages of tuberculosis (TB) medications for children with TB meningitis (TBM) during the 6-month intensive regimen (6HRZEto) are outlined. The short intensive TBM regimen involves higher doses per kilogram for isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide. 3. Following the recommendation for the short intensive TBM regimen, the World Health Organization (WHO) convened an expert consultation in October 2021 to discuss administration strategies using currently available child-friendly formulations. 4. The dose of isoniazid should be maintained at 15–20 mg/kg to prevent overexposure and potential toxicity. 5. Fixed-dose combination (FDC) child-friendly tablets are recommended over separate formulations for treating children with drug-susceptible TB. FDC tablets reduce pill burden, minimize prescription errors, and lower the risk of drug resistance by improving adherence. 6. Dispersible child-friendly FDC formulations for first-line TB medicines have been available since 2015. These can be dissolved in water to simplify and improve treatment. They are WHO-prequalified and represent improved formulations of existing first-line TB medicines. 7. For children weighing less than 25 kg, child-friendly dispersible tablet formulations, including HR FDC, are preferred. For children weighing 3–<5 kg, a joint ageand weight-based approach is used, considering maturation factors. 8. In the intensive phase of TB treatment, isoniazid 50 mg + rifampicin 75 mg + pyrazinamide 150 mg (HRZ 50/75/150 mg) is used. A dispersible formulation of ethambutol (E 100 mg) is also available. For the continuation phase, isoniazid 50 mg + rifampicin 75 mg (HR 50/75 mg) is used. 9. For children weighing 25–<35 kg, either dispersible tablets or adult formulations of the corresponding medicines can be used to reduce the pill burden. Severely ill children, such as those with reduced consciousness, can receive child-friendly dispersible formulations via a nasogastric tube. 10. Ethionamide can cause hepatotoxicity, gastrointestinal irritation, and hypothyroidism. Gastrointestinal irritation can often be mitigated by administering ethionamide in the evening, separate from other TB medicines. 11. For children weighing 3–<5 kg, dosing of RH and Z depends on whether the child is under or over 3 months of age. For those under 3 months, 5 tablets of Z 150 mg are used, while for those aged 3 months or older, 2 tablets of HR and 1 tablet of Z are used. 12. For children and adolescents weighing 25 kg or more, adult guidance and dose recommendations should be followed. These patients can be treated with adult formulations. Adolescents face unique challenges, such as peer pressure, stigma, comorbidities like HIV, and behaviors that complicate treatment, such as substance use. 13. Nutritional support is critical, as malnutrition reduces cell-mediated immunity, increasing susceptibility to TB. TB itself exacerbates weight loss and wasting, creating a vicious cycle. Severe malnutrition is associated with increased mortality in children and adolescents with TB. 14. Hepatotoxicity is a significant adverse event caused by TB medicines like isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide. Routine monitoring of serum liver enzyme levels is unnecessary unless clinical symptoms of hepatitis are present. If serum liver enzymes exceed five times the upper normal limit or three times with symptoms, hepatotoxic medicines should be stopped, and the patient should be referred to an expert. 15. In cases of severe hepatotoxicity, hospitalization may be necessary for close monitoring and management. Once liver function normalizes, ethambutol and rifampicin can be reintroduced first, followed by isoniazid. Pyrazinamide should not be reintroduced, and treatment with isoniazid, rifampicin, and ethambutol must continue for 9 months. 16. Peripheral neuropathy caused by isoniazid-induced pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency is characterized by pain, burning, tingling, numbness, or muscle cramps. In young children, it may manifest as gait changes or refusal to walk. Pyridoxine supplementation is recommended at 5–10 mg/kg/day, with higher doses (2–5 mg/kg/day) for persistent symptoms. 17. Ethambutol toxicity, including optic neuritis, is rare at WHO-recommended doses for a 2-month treatment duration. Monitoring for optic neuritis can be sought early if clinical concerns arise. Ethambutol should be used in TB treatment regimens for children of all ages as per WHO recommendations.
